docs.title: DASMixer user guide
docs.text:
DASMixer is a cross-platform desktop application for integrating and comparing peptide identification data from mass spectrometry experiments. It merges de novo sequencing results with library search identifications, performs full comparative proteomics workflows, and produces publication-ready reports.

Developed at the Laboratory of Structural Proteomics, IBMC, Moscow.

docs.title: Core concepts and formulas
docs.text: This note is important to avoid misunderstandings in terms used in DASMixer as they may not match any other terminology used by other proteomics software.

docs.title: Tool
docs.text: An instrument used to identify peptide sequences from spectre. Can be created by user and represents some source of Identifications (see below). Uses parser (or "importer") to parse input data format and transform it to internal representation of identification

docs.title: Sample
docs.text:
Proteomic sample of any source. Samples are created authomatically based on input spectra files. However single sample can contain more than one spectre file.

Features from two spectre files in the same Sample are directly combined, so it is not recommended to upload technical/biological repeats as different spectre files of the same sample. Consider using it for cases of fractioning or split processing.

docs.title: Specre
docs.text: Spectre for DASMixer is a single set of Mz and intensity values for a single precursor. Identifications must be matched to the precursor spectre to be calculatable and stored in the DASMixer project.

docs.title: Identification
docs.text:
Identification (widely known as PSM, peptide spectra match) is a peptide sequence matched to the Spectre using search engine and imported in DASMixer.

Identification is basically described with:

  • Tool used to get this identification
  • Peptide sequence in two forms:
  • sequence with described PTMs in HuPO ProForma notation with priority to named PTM form like [Phospho] or [Deamidated] instead of unreadable [UNIMOD:7]
  • canonical sequence with only canonical amino acids
  • search engine score
  • physical PSM characteristics

docs.title: Identification properties
docs.text:
DASMixer does not implement False Discovery statistical protocol. Instead, it calculates peptide fragmentation and analyze how it is mapped to the spectre.

Identifications mapping process performed with "Calculate Ion coverage" action. However, Ion Coverage is not the only one parameter calculating in this process.

These criteria follows:

docs.title: Intensity Coverage, %
docs.text:
Percent of total intensity of peacs in spectre to peaks associated with fragments.

\[Ic = \frac{\sum_{mz=0}^n i_{frag}}{\sum_{mz=0}^n i_{all}}*100\]

docs.title: PPM
docs.text:
Precursor error in parts per million, PPM error. Difference between precursor mass from spectre and theoretical mass of the identified sequence regarding PTMs and charge

\[PPM = \frac{Pepmass - MZ_{theor}}{MZ_{theor}} * 1e6\]

Where \(Pepmass\) is precursor mass reported along with spectra and \(MZ_{theor}\) calculated as follows:

\[MZ_{theor} = \frac{Mass_n + Charge * Proton}{Charge}\]

Where:

  • \(Mass_n\) is neutral monoisotopic mass of sequence with PTMs
  • \(Charge\) is precursor charge
  • \(Proton\) is a single proton mass constant (1.007276)

docs.title: Peaks covered, top peaks
docs.text: Number of peaks matched to ions. peaks covered is a simple metrics of how many fragments get matched to experimental spectra. Top peaks calculated as number of top-10 experimental spectra peaks matched to the fragments

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
Identification quality is an index of ions matched to the spectra. Based on:

Bern, M., Goldberg, D., McDonald, W. H., & Yates, J. R. (2004). Automatic Quality Assessment of Peptide Tandem Mass Spectra. Bioinformatics, 20(suppl_1), i49–i54. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bth947

\[Q = \frac{1}{N_{types}} * \frac{N_{match}}{L - 1}\]

Where:

  • \(N_{types}\) is number of ion types selected (2 if only b and y ions selected; up to 6 for a, b, c, x, y, and z)
  • \(N_{match}\) is number of unique ion matched. This value intentionnaly eexclude duplicates of fragment variations by charges and losses: y6, y6++ and y6-NH3 will count as single found fragment
  • \(L\) is length of peptide sequence.

docs.title: Longest Consequtive Run Ratio (LCRR)
docs.text:
An indicator of longest sequence of fragment ions found in the spectre and divided by sequence lenght. Can be described better by example:

Let's say, for a peptide consists of 10 amino acids, there are following fragments mapped to the experimental spectra:

y2, y3, y3++, y4-NH3, y6, y7, y9, b2, b4, b5, b7

LCRR value in this case will be equal to 0.3 as the longest conequtive run is of lenght 3 (y2, y3, y4) and peptide length is 10. y3 and y3++ considered as a single ion (like Quality calculation described above) and y5 is missing.

docs.title: Unconfirmed PTMs
docs.text:
Note: described logic is subject of refinement in further versions

Number of PTMs present in identification but not confirmed by fragmentation.

The fragment of the spectre corresponds to a partial sequence of the whole precursor peptide. As sequence is partial, it is common when overall fine covered sequence has no ion with sequence including one or more PTMs.

\[Unconfirmed = PTM(peptide) - \max_{i}(PTM({fragment_i}))\]

where fragment is fragment sequence, peptide is peptide sequence and PTM is function to calculate PTMs from ProForma record

docs.title: Spectre and identification correction
docs.text:
There are common problems with spectre metadata and sequence annotation that DASMixer tries to fix when calculating ion coverage:

  1. wrong or absent precursor charge of the spectra
  2. precursor mass error based on isotope offset
  3. fixed PTMs considered by search engine but not reported in sequence
  4. unlocalized PTMs (especially common for PLGS)

first two points can result in significant difference in theoretical and experimental precursor masses while 3rd and 4th affect fragment mapping.

DASMixer will try to: - minimize precursor PPM error iterating over charges and, for charge resulting in minimum absolute PPM, shifting mass for isotope offset; - recombinate PTMs in sequence to reach reasonable PPM error without decreasing intensity coverage

These steps are inkluded in pipeline by default yet can be easily omitted.

docs.title: Preferred identifications
docs.text:
Preferred identification is one of the most important concepts of DASMixer workflow and at the same time requires some effort to be understood.

It is obvious that not every identification can be trusted, especially if it is prodused by de novo search engine. Instead of calculating its own score or FDR value, DASMixer operates with set of criteria (described above) and user-defined thresholds for these criteria. Also while every identification is linked to the spectre, it is also important to not duplicate identifications used to estimate proteins abundance in sample. Preferred identification concept aimed to solve these two problems.

Identification can be considered preferred only if all its indicators passes thresholds set by user. If two or more identification of a single spectre passed thresholds, only the best one can be selected as preferred. If identifications are identical, preferred flag is set to first tool in list (it is not important when we speak about protein identification, however these identifications counted in Tool match report as found by "Both" tools).

In short: preferred identification is an identification that passes treshold of physical criteria for the tool and is better in spectre explanation than other identifications for this spectra.

Only preferred identifications are used to determine protein abundance. But preferred identifications not matched to the proteins can be additional point of interest representing unknown proteoforms or elements of peptidome. However, we recommend to thoroughly review such findings.

docs.title: Protein matching
docs.text:
For database search engines all the imported identifications are peptides taken from known proteins in proteome, while de novo search tools often provide only sequence without mapping to the proteins. DASMixer provides the tool to search identification sequences in user-provided proteome (via .fasta file upload). Uploading proteome to DASMixer is also useful if you are working with DB search only as identification data does not provide full protein sequences required to calculate protein coverage and theoretical peptides for LFQ.

Protein matching is performed using npysearch library:

Schmid S, Jeevannavar A, Julian TR, Tamminen M (2023) Portable BLAST-like algorithm library and its implementations for command line, Python, and R. PLoS ONE 18(11): e0289693. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0289693

Protein matching process is mandatory in pipeline, however for database search results it can just load proteins provided with identifications to project. This process is quite more important for de novo and open search scenarios.

docs.title: Protein identity
docs.text: Identity is a lower limit of match between identification sequence and most similar fragment in protein database. Identity can be in 0...1 interval where 1.0 is 100% match and 0.0 is just any aminoacid sequence.

docs.title: De Novo correction
docs.text:
DASMixer offers a de novo correction scenario to fix some portion of de novo sequencing errors. In this case, you should lower the protein identity setting and enable de novo correction mode for tool.

In that case, DASMixer searches peptides in protein database with difference until given identity. For de novo correction it is recommended to use identity in 0.7-0.8 interval.

The closest sequence found in protein database is called matched sequence. If identifications canonical sequence and matched sequence are not identical, DASMixer validates matched sequence against the experimental spectra: - calculates PPM difference. - calculates ion coverage with application of source PTMs. If PTM sites differs between sequence and matched sequence, DASMixer tries to re-allocate PTMs the same way it does for Ion matching

If ppm error and intensity coverage of matched sequence is not worse than the same indicators of original sequence, protein match is saved to the project.

If source sequence does not fit to preferred criteria while matched sequence does, DASMixer can consider this identification as preferred.

docs.title: Amino Acid substitutions
docs.text:
DASMixer can analyze if de novo identification contains potential amino acid substitution (AA substitution). AA substitution search is based on the same calculations that de novo correction, but relies on differen outcome.

AA substitution is suspected when: source sequence is fine enough to be considered preferred identification but protein match is not exact (identity < 1.0) and matched sequence has no better indicators of ppm and intensity coverage. In other words, sequence contains AA substitution if it slightly differs from canonical protein sequence but offers better explanation of the experimental spectre. You can see the example below:

AA substitution ion coverage example. First: fragmentation plot for sequence fond using PowerNovo2. Second: plot for matched sequence with identity=0.92. minor sequence changes results in loss of almost every y ion, significant PPM error increase and decrease of intensity coverage (iC)

Note: AA substitution search algorithm is experimental and can be subject of refinement in future versions of DASMixer. Correlation between de novo detected AA substitution and genetic mutations is not confirmed yet by proper publications. We recommend to thoroughly review AA substitution data presented by DASMixer before any conclusions are made.

docs.title: Unique evidences
docs.text: If sequence is found in one and only one protein in database, it is considered as unique evidence of protein existence in sample.

docs.title: Protein identifications
docs.text:
Based on list of preferred identifications matched to proteins, DASMixer creates a list of proteins in sample. Default limits to add protein in list are: - two identifications minimum - at least single unique evidence

These filters can be bypassed or strenghtened by user.

docs.title: Label-free quantification
docs.text: Label-free quantification (LFQ) is a set of approaches to estimate proteins proportion in complex mixture of the sample. DASMixer offers four different approaches to calculate LFQ and also two approaches to normalize these values by orthogonally calculated value. Methods described in details on Separate page

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
You can get the latest release from GitHub Releases.

Under the changelog in files section find the DASMixerX.X.X-setup.exe as shown below:

Follow the installation steps. DASMixer will be available to run as common desktop application and will be accessible via Start menu.

DASmixer project files .dasmix will also be associated with DASmixer app.

docs.title: Install as python package (other systems)
docs.text:
DASMixer can be installed as python package from PyPi repository:

pip install dasmixer

Alternatively, you can install CLI-mode only:

pip install dasmixer-cli

docs.title: Use Conda environment
docs.text:
DASMixer cannot be installed via Conda, but you can use COnda to create isolated environment. Recommended in older systems as DASmixer works best on Python 3.14

conda create -n dasmixer python=3.14 -y
conda activate dasmixer
pip install dasmixer

Pip installation can encounter some problems with dependency build. It can be easily solved using google search for missing system packages like libraries and compilers.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
DASMixer implements four label-free quantification methods at the protein level: emPAI, NSAF, iBAQ, and Top3. Each method estimates protein abundance from peptide-level data (spectral counts or intensities) without requiring isotopic labels.

LFQ results are calculated per sample and stored in the project. Both relative (normalized) and, optionally, absolute concentrations can be obtained.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text: Term Definition PSM Peptide-Spectrum Match — one identification of a peptide from one spectrum SpC Spectral Count — total number of PSMs assigned to a protein \(N_{\text{obs}}\) Number of unique (distinct) observed peptide sequences for a protein \(N_{\text{observ}}\) Number of theoretically observable peptides — obtained by in silico digestion of the protein sequence and filtering by length, mass, and missed cleavages Preferred identification The best identification per spectrum, selected across all tools

docs.title: emPAI — Exponentially Modified Protein Abundance Index
docs.text:
emPAI estimates protein abundance based on the ratio of observed to observable peptides. It was introduced by Ishihama et al. (2005) and is widely used in shotgun proteomics.

Formula:

\[\text{emPAI} = 10^{\,N_{\text{obs}} / N_{\text{observ}}} - 1\]

where the base \(10\) is the default; alternative bases (e.g., \(e\)) can be selected.

Key properties:

  • Uses only unique peptide sequences (duplicates are removed before counting \(N_{\text{obs}}\)).
  • \(N_{\text{observ}}\) is determined by in silico digestion of the protein with the chosen enzyme (default: trypsin, no missed cleavages), followed by peptide length filtering (default: 7–30 amino acids).
  • The output is a non-normalized index — higher emPAI means higher abundance.
  • The protein abundance (mol%) is estimated as:
\[\text{Protein content (mol\%)} = \frac{\text{emPAI}_i}{\sum_j \text{emPAI}_j} \times 100\%\]

DASMixer performs this normalization automatically and reports it as the relative value.

docs.title: NSAF — Normalized Spectral Abundance Factor
docs.text:
NSAF normalizes spectral counts by protein length and across all proteins in the sample. The underlying assumption is that larger proteins tend to generate more PSMs, so the count must be adjusted by protein size.

Step 1: SAF (Spectral Abundance Factor)

\[\text{SAF}_i = \frac{\text{SpC}_i}{L_i}\]

where \(\text{SpC}_i\) is the total PSM count for protein \(i\), and \(L_i\) is its sequence length in amino acid residues.

Step 2: NSAF (Normalized SAF)

\[\text{NSAF}_i = \frac{\text{SAF}_i}{\sum_j \text{SAF}_j}\]

The sum of all NSAF values in a sample equals 1. NSAF is the relative value reported by DASMixer.

Key properties:

  • NSAF uses spectral counts, not intensities — it does not require intensity data.
  • Normalization by protein length corrects for the bias that longer proteins generate more peptides and therefore more PSMs.
  • Works well for comparing protein abundances within a sample.

docs.title: iBAQ — Intensity-Based Absolute Quantification
docs.text:
iBAQ normalizes the total peptide intensity by the number of theoretically observable peptides. It was introduced by Schwanhäusser et al. (2011).

Formula:

\[\text{iBAQ}_i = \frac{\sum_k I_{i,k}}{N_{\text{observ}, i}}\]

where \(\sum_k I_{i,k}\) is the sum of intensities of all observed peptides assigned to protein \(i\) (including duplicates), and \(N_{\text{observ}, i}\) is the number of theoretically observable peptides.

Key properties:

  • Uses all peptide intensities — duplicates are included.
  • Peptides with missing intensity (NaN) are excluded from the sum.
  • \(N_{\text{observ}}\) is the same value used for emPAI (depends on digestion and filtering parameters).
  • Raw iBAQ is then normalized across proteins: \(\text{iBAQ}_{i,\text{norm}} = \text{iBAQ}_i / \sum_j \text{iBAQ}_j\).

docs.title: Top3 — Mean of Top 3 Peptide Intensities
docs.text:
Top3 approximates protein abundance as the arithmetic mean of intensities of the three most intense peptides assigned to the protein.

Formula:

\[\text{Top3}_i = \frac{I_{i,(1)} + I_{i,(2)} + I_{i,(3)}}{3}\]

where \(I_{i,(1)}, I_{i,(2)}, I_{i,(3)}\) are the three highest peptide intensities for protein \(i\), sorted in descending order.

Key properties:

  • Requires at least 3 peptides with intensity data. Proteins with fewer peptides receive no Top3 value.
  • Simple and robust — does not require theoretical digestion or sequence information.
  • Relies solely on MS1 intensity data.
  • Raw Top3 is then normalized across proteins: \(\text{Top3}_{i,\text{norm}} = \text{Top3}_i / \sum_j \text{Top3}_j\).

docs.title: Normalization (Relative Quantification)
docs.text:
For emPAI, iBAQ, and Top3, raw values are normalized so that they sum to 1 across all proteins in the sample:

\[v_{i,\text{norm}} = \frac{v_i}{\sum_j v_j}\]

This normalization produces relative abundance values, suitable for comparing protein levels within a single sample. NSAF is already normalized by definition (sum of SAF is 1).

docs.title: Absolute Quantification
docs.text: If a known protein concentration is available, DASMixer can convert relative values into absolute concentrations. Two approaches are supported:

docs.title: Total Protein Concentration
docs.text:
When the total protein concentration \(C_{\text{total}}\) is known (e.g., from a Bradford or BCA assay, in g/L):

\[C_{i,\text{mass}} = v_{i,\text{norm}} \times C_{\text{total}}\]

docs.title: Reference Protein (Internal Standard)
docs.text:
When the concentration of a specific reference protein \(C_{\text{ref}}\) is known:

\[C_{i,\text{mass}} = C_{\text{ref}} \times \frac{v_{i,\text{norm}}}{v_{\text{ref},\text{norm}}}\]

The reference protein is auto-detected by its UniProt accession (default: P02768, serum albumin), or can be specified manually.

docs.title: Combined Approach
docs.text:
When both \(C_{\text{total}}\) and \(C_{\text{ref}}\) are known, DASMixer combines them with a weighting factor \(\alpha\) (default \(0.5\)):

\[C_{i,\text{mass}} = \alpha \cdot C_{i,\text{mass}}^{\text{ref}} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot C_{i,\text{mass}}^{\text{total}}\]

docs.title: Conversion to Molar Concentrations
docs.text:
Mass concentrations (g/L) can be converted to molar units (mol/L):

\[C_{i,\text{molar}} = \frac{C_{i,\text{mass}}}{\text{MW}_i \times 1000}\]

where \(\text{MW}_i\) is the molecular weight of protein \(i\) in kDa (approximated as \(0.11 \times \text{length}\), i.e. average amino acid residue mass of 110 Da).

docs.title: Digestion Parameters
docs.text:
The calculation of \(N_{\text{observ}}\) (used by emPAI and iBAQ) depends on in silico digestion parameters:

Parameter Default Description Enzyme Trypsin Cleavage specificity for in silico digestion Min peptide length 7 Minimum amino acid residues in theoretical peptides Max peptide length 30 Maximum amino acid residues in theoretical peptides Missed cleavages 2 Maximum allowed missed cleavage sites

These parameters control which theoretical peptides are considered "observable" and directly affect emPAI and iBAQ values. Stricter filtering (tighter length range, fewer missed cleavages) reduces \(N_{\text{observ}}\) and increases the abundance index.

docs.title: Data Requirements
docs.text:
Method Requires FASTA Requires intensities Notes emPAI Yes No Needs protein sequence for in silico digestion NSAF Yes No Uses PSM counts and sequence length only iBAQ Yes Yes Needs both sequence and MS1 intensities Top3 No Yes Needs at least 3 peptide intensities

Only peptides from preferred identifications mapped to proteins are used. If intensity data is missing, iBAQ and Top3 will return no value for affected proteins.

docs.title: Running LFQ in DASMixer
docs.text:
LFQ is calculated via the Proteins tab in the GUI after: 1. Spectra and identifications have been imported 2. Preferred identifications have been selected 3. A FASTA database has been imported and protein mapping has been performed 4. Protein identification results have been computed

Select a sample, choose one or more LFQ methods, configure digestion parameters, and optionally enable absolute quantification by providing concentration values. The results are stored in the protein_quantification_result table and can be exported as CSV.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Ishihama, Y., et al. (2005). Exponentially Modified Protein Abundance Index (emPAI) for Estimation of Absolute Protein Amount in Proteomics by the Number of Sequenced Peptides per Protein. Molecular & Cellular Proteomics, 4(9), 1265–1272. DOI: 10.1074/mcp.M500061-MCP200

  2. Zybailov, B., et al. (2006). Statistical Analysis of Membrane Proteome Expression Changes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Journal of Proteome Research, 5(9), 2339–2347. DOI: 10.1021/pr060161n

  3. Schwanhäusser, B., et al. (2011). Global quantification of mammalian gene expression control. Nature, 473, 337–342. DOI: 10.1038/nature10098

  4. Silva, J. C., et al. (2006). Absolute Quantification of Proteins by LCMSE. Molecular & Cellular Proteomics, 5(1), 144–156. DOI: 10.1074/mcp.M500230-MCP200

docs.title: Calculate peptides and review identifications
docs.text:
Note: before proceed with this guide is highly recomended to read the Concepts page to understand the terms and indicators discussed below.

Peptides tab is composed from the set of functional blocks described in details below:

  • Actions
  • Protein sequence library
  • Ion match settings
  • Tool settings
  • Search and view identifications

docs.title: Common settings and actions
docs.text:
Actions section contains following buttons: - "Calculate peptides" to run the whole pipeline - Buttons to run separate subprocesses: - Select preferred - Calculate ion coverage - Match proteins to identifications - Save settings - Clear Calculations: deletes process results to allow recalculation

Protein sequence library allows user to import .fasta library of protein sequence to search. It also offers "Max accepts/Max rejects" settings to peptide search.

Ion matching settings is common configuration for all tools. These parameters allow to select ion types considered when calculating intensity coverage, fragment PPM threshold and fragment charges. Also settings in this field control spectre refinement: allowed charges to correct and maximum isotope offset value. Final part of this block is selection critera. If project contain identifications from multiple tools, this radio button defines what criteria will be used to select preferred identification for the spectre if there's more than one.

docs.title: Tool settings section
docs.text:
There is a tools settings displayed below. For every tool added to project, this section displays the same set of parameters.

Known minor issue: if tool was added and does not display in this section, simply close the project and open it again

Tool settings contain the following sections: - Main checkboxes - Preferred settings - PTM - Protein search

docs.title: Main tool checkboxes
docs.text: Main checkboxes are: - Trust all identifications: if selected, all the identifications provided by tool will be selected as preferred disregarding ion coverage and other criteria. They will be also always preferred against other identifications of the same spectra - Trust PPM: if checked, DASMixer will not overwrite ppm values loaded from identifications file - Use protein ID from file: DASMixer will not try to search given peptides in protein database and use protein ids imported from identifications file. Make sure that "Import protein IDs" checkbox were checked while identifications import for this tool. - Recalculate PTMs: enabled by default. If checked, DASMixer will try to recalculate PTMs in the identifications sequence if it does not pass PPM threshold.

docs.title: Preferred settings
docs.text:
Preferred settings block includes set of thresholds of reliability of identifications. They already have reasonable default values but can be fine-tuned by user. The list of controls with descriptions presented below:

Parameter Description Recommendedfor de novo Recommendedfor DB Max PPM Upper limit for absolute mass error in ppm 50 10 Min score Minimum search engine score¹ 0.7 0.0 Min ion Coverage (%) Minimum ion coverage for identification 15-25 15-25 Min peptide lenght Minimum lenght of the canonical sequence 5-7 7 Max peptide lenght Maximum lenght of the canonical sequence 30 30-45² Min top-10 peaks covered Minimum amount of top spectrum peaks covered by fragment ions 1 1 Min Ions covered Minimum amount of fragment matches 5-7 7 Min spectrum peaks Minimum total amount of peaks in spectrum 10 7-10³ Quality threshold Minimum Quality value 0.15-0.25 0.15-0.25 Min LCRR Minimum Longest Consequtive Run Ratio value 0.15-0.25 0.15-0.25 Max unconfirmed PTMs Maximum of PTMs not confirmed by ion fragmentation⁴ 1-2 1 Max FDR Max value for per-PSM FDR if it is reported by search engine 0.0 0.01 De novo correction Enables de novo correction for sequences found in proteins Yes No

Physical meaning and calculation formulas for these values described in Concepts page. Same with de novo correction. Notes: 1. DASMixer does not normalize search engine scores, so value depends on the values provided. For de novo engines its most common to use 0...1 values. For database search we recommend to disable score threshold (by setting 0.0) if results are loaded after FDR filtering. 2. Higher values of max peptide lenght can be recomended for engines known to worker well with longer peptides, mostly non-autoregression models such as PowerNovo2, Pi-Prime Nove. 3. Lower min spectrum peaks can be useful for DIA processing 4. Pasing with 1 skip is useful while Unconfirmed PTMs algorithm in DASMixer is not perfect yet. We recommend to lower this value if PTMs are subject of your research

docs.title: PTM Settings
docs.text: This settings section is enabled if you choose to Recalculate PTMs. It has controls: - Max PTM combinations: maximum PTMs that DASMixer can apply when processing the sequence. Increasing number can lead to better results but with cost of increase processing time - Select PTMs: allow user to change the list of PTMs DASMixer will try to apply for sequence refinement. "Amidated", "Deamidated" and "Pyridilethyl" are enabled by default. You can select more, but it will slower the processing. PTM configuration is described separately

docs.title: Protein search
docs.text:
Settings applied to protein match. Detailed in the table below:

Parameter Description Recommendedfor de novo Recommendedfor DB Min protein identity Minimum required identity between sequence of identification and sequence in protein DB 0.7-0.8 1.0 I/L combinatorics Consider leucine/isoleucine combination when matching proteins Yes No Match correction criteria List of criteria that allows DASMixer to trust matched sequence more than identified one PPM, Intensity coverage N/A Save AA substitutions Save "AA substitution" flag for sequences identified better than closest match in protein Yes No

docs.title: Important note about calculation time
docs.text:
Almost every setting parameter has correlation to one or more calculation processes performed by DASMixer. Processes are not equal by time-consumption and it should be considered by user. It also depend on amount of identifications.

Database search engines commonly produce identifications for about 20% of spectra in spectre file while de novo commonly produces identifications for almost every spectre in file (while about the same 20% can be trusted). Keep the amount of identifications imported im mind launching the processes.

If you have your DASMixer project stored at network storage or on HDD drive, it can also affect the timing of proceses. To increase processing time with cost of higher RAM usage, you can change batch size limits in system settings view.

Processes timings can be taken for here (for PC with 8 core CPU and M.2 SSD): - Ion matching: 3-5 minutes for 20000 identifications - Protein matching without de novo correction: 0.5-1 minutes for 20000 identifications - Protein matching with de novo correction/AA substitutions: 2-4 minutes for 20000 identifications - Preferred selection: 1-10 seconds per sample

Important conclusion: it is crucial for large projects to properly set the Ion matching parameters and protein search parameters before any calculations started as it can take hours to recalculate everyting in large project. But preferred selection thresholds can be a subject to refinement after the heavy calculations.

docs.title: Common process pipeline
docs.text:
You common order of actions is: 1. Open peptides tab 2. Import protein library 3. Adjust ion match parameters 4. Adjust tools parameters 5. Click "Calculate peptides" green button. 6. Wait until completed!

Calculation processing

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
When you run DASMixer, first you will see the main view with options to^ - Create new project - Open one of the recent projects opened in DASmixer (if there was any)

This screen also shows you the current version of DASMixer below the logo

docs.title: Project creation
docs.text:
Create project with "Create New Project" button. First, DASMixer will offer you to choose a location in your file system where your porjset file should be placed using standard filepicker.

Keep in mind: DASMixer project file contains copy of all the spectre data you are working with in zipped format, deflated to about 75%. The main consideration here: if you plan to work with, for example, 10GBs of MGF files, jou will need about 7.5GB free disk space for DASMixer project

When project is created, you can see the Project view:

Projct data and actions is split into 6 tabs: - Samples - Peptides - Proteins - Reports - Plots - Export

For now, project does not cantain any data except for default comparison group called "Control". It can be easily renamed and more groups can be added to this project Using "Add Group" button

docs.title: Working withcomparison groups (subsets)
docs.text:
You can add, edit and delete comparison groups (or "subsets" in DASMixer terms).

Technical note: "Subset" term has been choosen for technical representation because DASMixer project is SQLite database, and SQL language has reserved word "group". Using subset as table name makes internal queries more readable and writeable.

To add subset, click "Add group" button on the Samples tab. You will enter the "Add Comparison Group" dialog:

Here you can set name and description for the subset. You can also customize subset color: it will be used in plots when your research results will be compared between groups.

To edit created subset you can use the pencil (✏️) button near the group name with the same form.

Groups can be deleted using button with trash bin icon. However, only empty groups can be deleted, so you should first delete or move every sample from this group.

docs.title: Import spectral data
docs.text:
Next important step is spectra import. DASMixer currently supports only .MGF spectra import format. It is also recommended to import already processed deconvoluted, denoised and deisotoped .MGF files. Import start by clicking "Import spectra" button

There is two ways to import spectra: - By one file - Using pattern matching

One file is simple, you should just select file from file picker and (optionally) edit sample name. Pattern matching is more tricky.

First, you should select (or paste) path to the folder containing your MGF files. Then press "Preview files" button.

This dialog contains two fields for patterns: - File pattern: format to select files you want to import. in this pattern format, * symbol stands for any sequence of symbols. If you want to import every .MGF file in folder, default pattern *.mgf is fine. However if you want to get only files with name starts with "CNT_", you can correct this pattern to CNT*.mgf - Sample ID pattern: format to parse sample name from file name. substitute sample name part with {id}. Other variable parts can be substituted with {} and fixed parts can be added as is to the pattern. For example, if you have files named 20260912_S01_DDA.mgf and 20260914_S02_DDA.mgf, you can use pattern {}_{id}_DDA.mgf and store them as seamples S01 and S02 respectively.

Technical note for python enthusiasts: File pattern is passed to pathlib.Path.rglob() method while Sample ID pattern used with parse.parse() function.

After adjusting patterns, you should always check if mapping fits your expectations by clicking "Preview files" and look at the changes in list below. You can manually rename samples and deselect files you don't want to import.

If everything is OK, press the "Import" button and wait for the spectra to be imported:

Modal dialog will disappear when import is done.

docs.title: Create tool and import identifications
docs.text:
Next step is to create tool(s) by clicking "Add tool"

Tool is a search engine wich results you want to import. Setings dialog includes: - Tool name - Tool type (database/de novo) - Parser: type of input files you work with. Selected from supported sources - Color (used in reports)

When tool is created, you can see the list of tools in project and press "Import identifications" button for one of the tools. Import process i commonly the same as for spectre import but pattern adjusting is more important.

Most of the engines provides results as set of files with the same filename extensions but different prefixes, so it should be difined. For instance, PowerNovo2 creates several CSV files with different data details. Identifications can be imported from *_denovo.csv files only. The same is fair to PLGS: you should import *_peptide.csv files.

Hint: If files stored in complex folder tree, like /your-data-root/comparison_group/denovo_output/sample_01/sample_01_denovo.csv, you can set only file name pattern and import path to /your-data-root/. Potential problem: if results are stored in structure like /experiment/sample01/denovo.tsv (same filenames in every folder) you will have to rename files before import or import manually file per file

After data is imported, you can add another tool (e.g. MaxQuant), validate imports on "Manage samples" view or proceed to Peptides tab to view data and perform calculations

docs.title: MaxQuant Import
docs.text: DASMixer can import full MaxQuant search results directly into an existing project. The importer reads mqpar.xml (configuration), msms.txt / msmsScans.txt (identification metadata), and .apl peak-list files, then converts them into regular spectra and identifications inside your .dasmix project.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Your MaxQuant output must include:

File / folder Expected location (relative to mqpar.xml) Purpose mqpar.xml anywhere (you select it) Paths and RAW file list msms.txt <txt_folder>/msms.txt Peptide identifications msmsScans.txt <txt_folder>/msmsScans.txt Scan metadata {raw_name}/p0/*.apl <raw_parent>/{raw_name}/p0/*.apl Peak lists (one per sample) .fasta <fasta_file> (optional) Protein sequences

<txt_folder>, <raw_parent>, and <fasta_file> are parsed automatically from mqpar.xml. You can override them in the GUI or via CLI options.

Note: only per-sample .apl files (<raw_name>/p0/*.apl) are supported. combined/andromeda/*.apl files (mixed spectra without sample assignment) are not imported.

If mqpar.xml references multiple RAW-file parent directories, only the first one is used. Put all RAW samples in a single directory for best results.

docs.title: 1. Open the dialog
docs.text: Switch to the Samples tab. You will see a new Import From MaxQuant section next to the existing Import Spectra block. Click Import From MaxQuant….

docs.title: 2. Select mqpar.xml
docs.text: Click Browse, choose your mqpar.xml file, then click Parse. The importer will extract all paths and RAW-file names from the XML.

docs.title: 3. Configure paths
docs.text:
The dialog shows three path fields with status icons:

  • RAW files path — folder containing {raw_name}/p0/ subdirectories.
  • Custom TXT folder — folder containing msms.txt and msmsScans.txt.
  • FASTA file — protein database (optional).

Click the folder icon next to each field to browse. The icon turns green when the path is valid, red otherwise.

The Import button stays disabled until all validations pass.

docs.title: 4. Choose options
docs.text:
Option Default Description Tool name MaxQuant Name of the identification tool in your project Subset name MaxQuant Import Comparison group for imported samples Import proteins from FASTA file on If enabled, protein sequences are imported Sequences are in UniProt format on Parses UniProt-style headers >sp\|...\|... Delete temporary files after import on Removes intermediate MGF/CSV files Skip contaminant identifications on Filters out Potential contaminant rows On duplicates Skip What to do if a file was already imported

Decoy identifications (Decoy = +) are always excluded, regardless of the contaminant checkbox.

docs.title: 5. Select RAW files
docs.text: The list at the bottom shows every RAW file from mqpar.xml. Uncheck any samples you want to skip. Use Select All / Deselect All for quick control.

docs.title: 6. Run import
docs.text:
Click Import. The dialog switches to a progress screen showing:

Processing CRC_Rep1 (1/10)
████████░░░░░░░░░░░░  10%
Stage: spectra

Import cannot be cancelled once started (this ensures data consistency).

When finished, the dialog closes and a green snack-bar summarizes the results:

MaxQuant import complete: 10 sample(s), 50 000 spectra, 12 340 identifications

The new samples, files, and identifications appear immediately in the Samples tab and are ready for downstream analysis.

docs.title: CLI Import
docs.text:
dasmixer-cli import maxquant PROJECT_PATH MQPAR_PATH [OPTIONS]

If PROJECT_PATH does not exist, a new project is created automatically.

docs.title: Required arguments
docs.text: Argument Description PROJECT_PATH Path to .dasmix file (created if missing) MQPAR_PATH Path to mqpar.xml

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description --fasta-path from mqpar.xml Override FASTA file path --raw-path from mqpar.xml Override RAW files parent directory --txt-path from mqpar.xml Override txt results folder path --tool-name MaxQuant Tool name --subset-name MaxQuant Import Subset (group) name --keep-contaminants off Keep Potential contaminant identifications --import-fasta / --no-import-fasta --import-fasta Import proteins from FASTA --fasta-uniprot / --fasta-generic --fasta-uniprot FASTA headers are UniProt-formatted --delete-temporary-files / --keep-temporary-files --delete-temporary-files Remove intermediate MGF/CSV files --on-duplicates skip skip | reload | add_as_new

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
dasmixer-cli import maxquant /data/my_project.dasmix /data/mq/mqpar.xml \
    --tool-name MaxQuant --subset-name "MaxQuant Import"

CLI output shows per-stage progress:

  [metadata] Reading metadata...
  [converting] Converting CRC_Rep1.HCD.FTMS.peak.apl...
  [converting] Converting CRC_Rep2.HCD.FTMS.peak.apl...
  [creating_tool_subset] Setting up subset and tool...
  [spectra] Processing CRC_Rep1 (1/10)
  [spectra] Processing CRC_Rep2 (2/10)
  ...
  [done] Saving project...
  ...
Import complete: 10 sample(s), 50000 spectra, 12340 identifications

docs.title: What Happens During Import
docs.text:
1. Read metadata — msms.txt and msmsScans.txt are loaded into memory.
  2. Convert APL → MGF — each .apl file is parsed and written as a temporary .mgf file enriched with sequence, charge, and retention-time annotations from the metadata. A companion .csv identification file is generated in the same temp directory.

Temporary files are stored under ~/.cache/dasmixer/tmp/maxquant_import/<timestamp>/ and deleted when the import finishes (unless you uncheck "Delete temporary files").

  1. Create tool and subset — a MaxQuant tool (type Library, parser MaxQuant) and a MaxQuant Import comparison group are created in your project if they don't already exist.

Important: if a tool named MaxQuant already exists but has a different parser, the import is blocked (GUI: button stays grey; CLI: hard error). Rename the existing tool before retrying.

  1. Import proteins (optional) — the FASTA file is parsed and protein entries are added to the database.

  2. Import spectra and identifications per sample — for each RAW file:

  3. A sample is created (or reused if the name already exists).
  4. Each .mgf file is imported as spectra.

  5. Each companion .csv is imported as identifications linked to the MaxQuant tool.

  6. Save — the project is checkpointed.

docs.title: Re-importing / Duplicates
docs.text:
You can run the same import multiple times. The behaviour depends on the On duplicates setting:

Setting Behaviour Skip (default) Existing spectra/identification files are skipped Reload Existing files are deleted and re-imported Add as new New records are created alongside old ones

Samples with matching names are always reused — a second sample with the same name is never created.

docs.title: After Import
docs.text:
Imported data is immediately available:

  • Samples appear in the Samples tab under the chosen subset.
  • Spectra are linked to the sample's spectre_file records.
  • Identifications are linked to the MaxQuant tool and can be used for preferred-identification selection, protein mapping, and quantification.

The regular DASMixer analysis pipeline (ion coverage, preferred identifications, protein mapping, LFQ, reports) works on MaxQuant-imported data exactly as on data imported through standard spectra/identification imports.

docs.title: Limitations (Current Version)
docs.text:
• Only per-sample .apl files ({raw_name}/p0/) are supported. Shared combined/andromeda/*.apl files are not importable.
  • If .apl files are spread across multiple RAW-parent directories, only the first one listed in mqpar.xml is used.
  • Import cannot be cancelled once started.
  • proteinGroups.txt, summary.xml, and other MaxQuant output files are not imported (future enhancement).
  • Debug option --limit from the old mq2dasmix utility is not available.

docs.title: PTM Configuration
docs.text: DASMixer maintains its PTM (post-translational modification) definitions in two plain-text CSV files located in the application configuration directory. You can inspect and edit these files to add new modifications or to teach DASMixer how to recognise PTM notation from third-party software.

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
All PTM configuration files live in:

OS Path Linux ~/.config/dasmixer/ptm/ Windows %APPDATA%/dasmixer/ptm/ macOS ~/Library/Application Support/dasmixer/ptm/

The folder is created automatically on the first DASMixer launch. You can open it quickly from the application:

Settings → click Open configuration folder.

This opens the entire dasmixer config directory in your system file manager; the ptm/ subfolder is inside it.

docs.title: all_ptm_config.csv — PTM definitions
docs.text:
This file lists all modifications that DASMixer can try when searching for fixed PTMs on peptide sequences. Each row defines one modification.

Columns:

Column Type Description name text PTM identifier shown in the UI (e.g. Oxidation, Deamidated) attach_to text Amino-acid codes the PTM can attach to, separated by ; (e.g. S;T;Y). Leave empty for terminal-only or unrestricted PTMs. mono_mass number Monoisotopic mass shift (Da). Leave empty to look up the mass from the built-in Unimod database automatically. n_term Y/N Whether this PTM can appear at the protein N-terminus. c_term Y/N Whether this PTM can appear at the protein C-terminus. default Y/N If Y, this PTM is pre-selected in the tool settings dialog when no explicit PTM list has been saved.

Default set: 43 common PTMs are shipped with DASMixer. Three of them have default=Y: Amidated, Deamidated, Pyridylethyl. These are the modifications enabled by default for new tools.

docs.title: import_ptm_renames.csv — parser aliases
docs.text:
Identification files from third-party software (MaxQuant, PLGS, PeptideShaker) use their own notation for modifications. This file maps those vendor-specific names to the standard DASMixer PTM codes used in all_ptm_config.csv.

Columns:

Column Type Description source text Substring in the identification file that should be replaced (e.g. (Deamidation (NQ)), S-pyridylethyl) proforma text Target PTM code (must match a name in all_ptm_config.csv) or a ProForma string (e.g. [Deamidated], [-89.029920]- for N-terminal acetylation). parser text Which parser this rule applies to: MaxQuant, PLGS, or PeptideShaker XLS. is_terminal Y/N Whether this substitution represents a terminal modification (N-term or C-term). Y only for positional PTMs like NH2 → Amidated.

Default set: 18 entries covering all three supported parsers.

docs.title: Important rules
docs.text:
1. CSV format only. Both files must remain valid CSV with the header row intact. All columns are required; empty cells are allowed where noted above.

  2. Encoding. Files use UTF-8 encoding without BOM. Most text editors handle this automatically.

  3. Changes take effect on restart. DASMixer reads these files once at startup. After editing, restart the application.

  4. PTM codes are case-sensitive. Oxidation and oxidation are different identifiers. Always match the exact spelling.

docs.title: Recommended editors
docs.text: Editor Notes LibreOffice Calc File → Open → choose all_ptm_config.csv. In the import dialog set Separator: Comma, Text delimiter: ". After editing, File → Save As → choose CSV format, check Edit filter settings, make sure Field delimiter: ,, String delimiter: ", Quote all text cells: No. OpenOffice Calc Same procedure as LibreOffice. Microsoft Excel File → Open → choose the CSV file. Important: Excel may interpret values like Methylthio or Glu->pyro-Glu incorrectly. After editing, use File → Save As → CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited) (*.csv). The attach_to column with ; separators will be quoted automatically — that is correct. VS Code / Notepad++ / any text editor Simplest option: edit as plain text. Install a CSV syntax-highlighting extension for readability.

docs.title: Adding a new PTM
docs.text:
1. Open all_ptm_config.csv.
  2. Append a new row at the bottom (or insert anywhere). Example: MyNewPTM,K,16.0,Y,N,N This defines a PTM called MyNewPTM that attaches to lysine (K), has mass +16.0 Da, can be N-terminal, not C-terminal, and is not a default PTM.
  3. Save the file and restart DASMixer.
  4. The new PTM will appear in the Select PTMs dialog (Peptides tab → Tool Settings → PTM → Select PTMs…).

docs.title: Adding a parser alias
docs.text:
1. Open import_ptm_renames.csv.
  2. Append a new row. Example for MaxQuant: (MyCustomMod),MyNewPTM,MaxQuant,N This tells DASMixer: when importing MaxQuant evidence files, replace the substring (MyCustomMod) in the Modified Sequence column with MyNewPTM.
  3. Save and restart. The alias is picked up on the next identification import.

docs.title: Resetting to defaults
docs.text: If you ever need to restore the original configuration, simply delete the ptm/ folder (or the specific CSV file) and restart DASMixer. The application will regenerate the files from built-in defaults on the next startup.

docs.title: In peptide matching
docs.text:
When DASMixer performs ion-coverage calculation and PTM fixing (seqfixer), it uses the PTMS list loaded from all_ptm_config.csv. For each peptide sequence it tries all enabled PTMs in the configured combinations (up to max_ptm simultaneous modifications) to find a match within the PPM tolerance.

The set of enabled PTMs is configured per tool in the GUI:

Peptides tab → Tool Settings → PTM → Select PTMs…

The dialog shows all 43 PTMs with their sites and mass. Three are pre-selected by default. You can enable or disable any combination.

docs.title: In identification import
docs.text: When importing identification files, DASMixer uses import_ptm_renames.csv to convert vendor-specific modification notation to standard ProForma format. This happens automatically — no user action required beyond keeping the renames file up to date if you use custom PTM notation in your source files.
